paragraphs.heading: What botanists mean by fruit
paragraphs.text: In botany, a fruit is the part of a flowering plant that carries the seeds, formed from the ovary after the plant flowers. It is how flowering plants, or angiosperms, spread their seeds. Put simply, a fruit is a ripened ovary that holds seeds, while a seed is a ripened ovule. That makes a nut a kind of fruit, not a seed.

paragraphs.heading: Kitchen words and plant words
paragraphs.text: In the kitchen, fruit usually means fleshy produce, sweet or sour, that can be eaten raw, such as apples, grapes and oranges, while vegetables tend to be savoury. Botany counts far more as fruit, including nuts, bean pods, corn kernels, tomatoes and wheat grains. Cucumbers, pumpkins, peas, bell peppers and eggplants are botanical fruits that are usually called vegetables, and spices such as black pepper and cumin are fruits too. Rhubarb works the other way: it goes into pies as a fruit, but the part people eat is the leaf stalk.

paragraphs.heading: Why fruits matter
paragraphs.text: Edible fruits and animals, humans included, help each other: the animals get food and the plants get their seeds spread. Many animals, people among them, now depend on fruit for food, so fruit makes up a large share of the world's farm output. Some fruits, such as the apple and the pomegranate, also carry rich cultural and symbolic meaning. Cereal grains such as rice and wheat are fruits as well, called caryopses, but the fruit wall is thin and joined to the seed coat, so nearly all of the grain is really seed.

paragraphs.heading: How a fruit begins
paragraphs.text: A fruit comes from the fertilizing and ripening of one or more flowers. At the centre of the flower sits the gynoecium, with its stigma, style and ovary, and it forms all or part of the fruit; the ovary holds one or more ovules. Pollination moves pollen from the stamens to the stigma, and a pollen tube then grows down the style to an ovule and delivers two sperm. One joins the egg to form a zygote, which becomes the seed's embryo. The other enters a central cell that goes on to make endosperm, a food tissue for the embryo, and the whole process is called double fertilization.

paragraphs.heading: The fruit wall
paragraphs.text: As the ovules turn into seeds, the ovary ripens, and its wall, the pericarp, becomes the outer layer of the fruit. It may turn fleshy, as in berries and drupes, or hard, as in nuts. The pericarp usually has two or three layers: the exocarp or epicarp outside, the mesocarp in the middle and the endocarp inside. In some species, tissues other than the ovary help form the part we eat.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of fruit
paragraphs.text: In some fruits the petals, stamens and other flower parts drop away as the fruit ripens. Where the ovary sits below the other floral parts, though, some of those parts fuse with it and ripen too. When such parts make up a significant share of the fruit, it is called an accessory fruit, such as an apple, strawberry or pineapple. Plant scientists sort fruits into three main groups that match how they develop: simple, aggregate and multiple. Simple fruits come from a single flower, while multiple fruits come from many flowers grouped together.
